title: Noise increases memory in pathway models, especially associative memory

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Noise increases memory in pathway models, especially associative memory

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Adding stochastic noise to simulations of the surveyed ODE pathway models left memories intact in most models (83%) and increased memory overall by about 20%, most notably associative memory, suggesting that biological noise does not inhibit and may help the trainability of such networks.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: Learning in Transcriptional Network Models: Computational Discovery of Pathway-Level Memory and Effective Interventions

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Biswas S 2022, Learning in Transcriptional Network Models: Computational Discovery of Pathway-Level Memory and Effective Interventions › 2. Results › 2.3. Memory Effects Are Robust to Noise

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: Interestingly, while almost all models retained the memories created (83%), there was an overall 20% increase in memory in the presence of noise (averaged across models and memory phenotypes) most notably in the associative memory paradigm.

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Biswas S, Clawson W, Levin M, “Learning in Transcriptional Network Models: Computational Discovery of Pathway-Level Memory and Effective Interventions”, International journal of molecular sciences (2022), doi:10.3390/ijms24010285; section “2. Results › 2.3. Memory Effects Are Robust to Noise”. Scope: 35 ODE pathway models from BioModels with added stochasticity

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on levin-2022-grn-learning-10: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.83

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The simulation result can be checked using public models and a specified perturbation. The biological interpretation is narrower than the numerical result because alternative noise processes may behave differently.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Reproduce the stated stochastic perturbation, run sufficient random seeds, and compare memory retention and type-specific counts against deterministic runs. Confidence intervals around the 83% and 20% summaries determine replication.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
A model-level increase does not show that biological noise helps real pathways.

Results depend on the noise model and amplitude.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data adequacy: 0.8
data existence: 0.88
discriminating power: 0.78
operationalizability: 0.93
analysis feasibility: 0.75

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: A public noise script can recheck the 83 percent retention and the 20 percent increase inside this simulation. The claim also treats that stochasticity as evidence about biological noise and trainability, which this single noise process does not separate from an artifact of the integrator. The numerical half is testable; the biological reading is not.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Rerun the memory assays with the repository's stochastic perturbation and compare per-type memory counts with the deterministic runs. Retention in about 83 percent of models and a roughly 20 percent rise, largest for associative memory, would reproduce the numerical claim; a drop, or a rise concentrated in another memory type, would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
One added-noise scheme is not biological noise in cells, so the therapeutic suggestion is not identified.

The 20 percent average depends on how memory phenotypes are pooled.
